li.a: Police Magazine: The Black Guerrilla Family Prison Gang
Jacobin: Black Radical Prisoner Organizing Didn't Die With George Jackson
Corrections1: Corrections officer sentenced in BGF gang racketeering conspiracy at Baltimore jail
Federal Criminal Defense Attorney blog: 24 Guards Among 40 Convicted in Baltimore City Jail Scandal
WBAL: Gov. Hogan Announces Closing Of Baltimore City Men's Detention Center
Baltimore Sun: Baltimore police say gangs 'teaming up' to take out officers

content.p: The Black Guerrilla Family, usually shortened to BGF, began as a political project behind prison walls and has been prosecuted as a criminal organization. Writers who study it describe it as the product of the Black Power movement meeting the California prison system. The police and prosecutors quoted here know it through drug cases, jail smuggling and violence. Both pictures rest on real events, and the sources that describe them often disagree on emphasis, so this account attributes each claim to whoever made it.

Two episodes anchor the story. One is the life and death of George Jackson, the man credited with founding the group. The other is a 2013 federal racketeering case in Baltimore, in which prosecutors said the gang had effectively taken over parts of a state jail with the help of the officers paid to guard it.

Police Magazine and the Baltimore Sun both date the group's start to 1966, when George Jackson was held at San Quentin, in northern California. The Baltimore Sun adds that Jackson was serving time for an armed robbery conviction. Police Magazine, in an article by a former sergeant who led a surveillance team in a 1987 drug case, describes him as a former Black Panther and an excellent orator who rallied inmates by speaking about the injustice of the system, especially to Black prisoners. By that account he believed the Panthers were not radical enough and did not represent imprisoned Black men well, and he vowed to build an organization that would support them like a family and act as a vanguard in a coming revolution against the U.S. government.

The same article says the group was first called the Family or the Black Family, and was also known as the Black Vanguard and the Black Foco. It says lawyers and paralegals from the National Lawyers Guild helped to write the group's constitution, which it describes as built on a paramilitary ranking system and Marxist-Maoist politics. Swahili was used in much of the group's internal communication, Police Magazine reports, and leaders took Swahili names alongside their own names and gang monikers. New members, it says, had to memorize and recite an oath.

The Jacobin article gives the origin a different frame and a slightly different date. Citing the sociologist Brittany Friedman, it says Jackson and others founded the Black Guerilla Family in 1970, a revolutionary cadre-building organization meant to be the prison arm of the Black Power movement. It places the founding just after the killing of W. L. Nolen on 13 January 1970. Nolen, it says, was widely respected by other prisoners for his intelligence and political leadership, and was shot dead in a Soledad State Prison yard, after officers, it says, engineered a confrontation with "Nazi prisoners". The article says a grand jury acquitted the officers responsible a few months later, and that a different Soledad officer was then killed, in what it describes as apparent retaliation. The officer's murder was then charged against Jackson and two other Black militants, despite what Jacobin calls a dearth of evidence. The sources therefore give 1966 and 1970 as the group's starting point, and neither page resolves the difference.

On 21 August 1971, according to Jacobin, correctional officers shot and killed the 29-year-old Jackson in the San Quentin yard. The event killed two other incarcerated people and three correctional officers, in Jacobin's count. The Baltimore Sun gives the toll as five others dead alongside Jackson and says Jackson was armed with a pistol when he was killed. It adds that he was awaiting trial on a charge that he had murdered a prison guard. Jacobin ranks him among the best-known political leaders in California's prisons at the time and notes he had been locked up since the age of 21.

Police Magazine, a law-enforcement trade publication, describes the day as an attempted escape. It says a lawyer was suspected of bringing in the weapons used, and that Mexican Mafia members used weapons and killed prison guards during the incident. The page names no conviction for those men and gives no court record. It also notes that Bob Dylan recorded a song called "George Jackson." The account is one former officer's account, written from a policing point of view, and its wording about Jackson is hostile, so the circumstances of the shooting should be read as one side's description rather than a settled finding.
content.h2: Splits, rivals and the drug trade
content.p: After Jackson, Police Magazine says, a former Symbionese Liberation Army leader nicknamed Doc Holiday became the next supreme commander. Under him the gang grew in power and numbers, recruiting from the Crips and Bloods who were imprisoned in the 1980s. The article says the gang maintained a revolutionary militant faction and a criminal faction aimed at personal gain that still supported the cause. It lists several rival factions that grew up against recognized leaders, among them a group that took the old Vanguard name in 1978 at Deuel Vocational Institute and opposed both the revolutionary politics and the severe methods used to purge the ranks. That group declared war on the BGF at Folsom Prison in 1979, the article says, and in 1981 the BGF moved against it, killing one person and injuring several others. The article also says a group called the Black August Organizing Committee formed inside the BGF in 1977, in the Bay Area, to unite Black people in West Coast gangs on the street and in prison.

The same article makes a claim about recruitment that investigators would have found hard to prove: that the BGF recruited covertly from Crips, Bloods and other groups and encouraged members to keep claiming their earlier affiliation, so that gang investigators could not easily identify them. This is the writer's assertion and the page cites no document for it.

The author of the Police Magazine article, a former sergeant who led a surveillance team, describes one large operation. Operation Sting Ray, he says, was a multi-agency task force led by the Drug Enforcement Administration against cocaine and crack dealers, with officers briefed on 30 June 1987 for the warrant service. He says 44 people were eventually indicted and that 19 were arrested that first day, among them Elrader "Ray Ray" Browning, the head of a drug organization, and Doc Holiday, whom he calls the BGF's supreme commander. Authorities seized more than 15 pounds of crack and powder cocaine, more than $300,000 in cash and 10 vehicles, he writes, and seized more than $13 million in property and bank accounts for forfeiture. He also says the two men were later convicted in federal court and received life sentences, and that a key informant was abducted from her apartment and murdered within a week of the arrests. These details come from a single participant's recollection, and the page does not link to court records.

A Maryland case surfaced in 2009, when a Baltimore Sun piece described two BGF indictments returned that April by the U.S. Attorney's Office in Maryland. A 122-page book, The Black Book: Empowering Black Families and Communities, was at the center of the argument. The Sun says the inmate Eric Marcell Brown, then 40, wrote much of it, and that he and his wife, Deitra Davenport, had incorporated a publishing company to print and sell it. Brown, Davenport and 23 other co-defendants named in the two indictments were accused of drug dealing, prison smuggling, violence and extortion, according to the Sun, and prosecutors said the book was a recruiting tool whose sales also helped to pay for the gang's crimes. Assistant U.S. Attorney James Wallner made the profit claim in court, the paper reports.

Others disagreed. Tyrone Powers, a former FBI agent and Maryland State Police trooper who directs a homeland security and criminal justice institute, had endorsed the book on its back cover. He told the Sun the book was positive and aimed at reducing violence, and that he did not know anything about its financing. Davenport's lawyer, Thomas Saunders, argued there was no profit once printing costs were counted and that his client used her own money. The book itself, the Sun says, calls itself a "living policy book" and honors Jackson's vision. The article quotes passages on gender roles, including advice on disciplining a disobedient wife, that the Sun described in plain terms. Whether the book was propaganda or self-help was a question for the court and this source does not report a ruling on it.
content.h2: The Baltimore City Detention Center case
content.p: The most heavily documented case involves the Baltimore City Detention Center, a state-run jail. A sweeping federal indictment announced in April 2013 alleged that Tavon "Bulldog" White directed a BGF operation that brought in contraband, from cell phones and tobacco to prescription pills and other drugs, which gang members sold at a profit. The first indictment named White, 13 jail guards and 11 other prisoners. A second indictment, made public that November, named a further 14 guards and six others, bringing the total to 44 defendants, according to the Federal Criminal Defense Attorney blog.

White pleaded guilty on 6 August 2013 to one count of racketeering. He admitted heading the BGF at the jail and conspiring with guards. According to the same page he also admitted fathering children with female guards, and four guards named in the indictment were reported pregnant by him, two of whom had his name tattooed on their bodies. Authorities alleged he took power soon after arriving at the jail in 2009 to await trial on attempted second-degree murder, a charge that ended with two hung juries before a sentence of 20 years, the blog says. A recorded phone call presented to a federal grand jury has White saying he made nearly $16,000 in a single slow month. In other calls recorded by investigators he declared "This is my jail" and said everything had to go through him, according to transcripts the blog quotes.

The guards were central. Court records, the blog says, alleged that BGF members recruited officers through personal and often sexual relationships and through bribes, and that some officers traded sex for money. Officers carried in contraband that they concealed on their bodies, and the chance of being searched was remote, prosecutors said. U.S. Attorney Rod Rosenstein said the corruption let those involved earn large sums through drug trafficking, extortion, bribery and other crimes. The FBI's Stephen Vogt put it this way: "the inmates literally took over the asylum." The defense at the trial of eight remaining defendants attacked White's credibility as a government witness. Defense lawyer Richard Bardos told the jury that under the plea agreement White's 12-year federal term would run concurrently with his state sentence. Bardos went further and claimed the corruption was "state-approved, state-facilitated, and administratively encouraged." That was an argument made at trial, not a finding.

Sentences followed. Corrections1 reported in February 2014 that former officer Jasmine Thornton, 26, was sentenced to 32 months for smuggling marijuana, tobacco and prescription pills during six years at the jail, warning inmates of searches according to her plea deal, and having a sexual relationship with a prisoner, according to court documents. She was the third officer sentenced, after Taryn Kirkland and Adrena Rice, who were each serving 42 months. The jail's top BGF leader besides White, Steven Loney, was sentenced to nine years after pleading guilty. By April 2015, of 44 people charged, 35 had pleaded guilty and one had died.

On 30 July 2015, Maryland governor Larry Hogan announced that the Baltimore City Men's Detention Center would close at once. He called it "the worst jail in America" and said inmates "were literally running this prison." WBAL reported at that time that 40 of the 44 defendants had been convicted, including 24 correctional officers, and that White had been sentenced to 12 years. The ACLU and the Public Justice Center had separately asked a federal judge to reopen a lawsuit over conditions at the jail. The state's corrections secretary, Stephen Moyer, said the state had spent more than $58 million over a decade on safety and security.

Concern about the gang outside the walls surfaced the same year. In April 2015, while demonstrations over the death of Freddie Gray were under way, Baltimore Police said they had received a credible threat that gangs including the Black Guerrilla Family, Bloods and Crips had entered into a partnership to harm officers. The Sun reported that a spokesman could not say how the information was received and would not say whether it was linked to the demonstrations. It also reported that an FBI memo in December 2014 relayed a contact's claim that BGF members planned to target white officers, and that in January a man carrying a handgun entered a Baltimore police station and said it was a security test ordered by the BGF. These were reports of threats and statements. The pages do not say any attack followed.
